One map has a color outlier: France gets ~67% of its electricity from nuclear power. Its neighbors don't come close.

This wasn't geology. France has no unusual uranium, no special engineering gene.

It was one decision, made in a single week in 1974 — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ 1973: the oil embargo hits. France imports ~75% of its energy, almost all of it oil — no North Sea fields like Britain, no coal seams like Germany. The shock was closer to an emergency than an inconvenience.

2/ March 6, 1974: PM Pierre Messmer announces a plan to build 44 reactors, enough to run almost the whole country on nuclear. Decided in the Cabinet — no public vote, barely any debate. ~4,000 scientists signed a protest petition anyway.
3/ France didn't reinvent the wheel, it standardized it. One licensed reactor design, built over and over by Framatome. 56 reactors in ~15 years — about one new unit every three months.

4/ The payoff shows up on a completely different map: carbon intensity. France's grid runs ~56g CO2/kWh. Germany's, after phasing out nuclear post-Fukushima, runs ~371g — six times dirtier, despite huge wind and solar spending.

5/ The bet wasn't free: unresolved waste storage, an aging fleet whose corrosion problems idled over half of it in 2022, and a new flagship reactor (Flamanville) that arrived 6x over budget and 12 years late.

6/ France doubled down anyway. In Feb 2022, Macron announced 6 new reactors, with 8 more possible. The 'nuclear map' isn't really about geology — it's a map of which governments made one big bet 50 years ago and never walked it back.

Full story — the 1974 decision, the Germany comparison, the 2022 gamble — in this week's Lines & Legends, free every 3 days: https://buttondown.com/forummapping

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this 🗺️
